output: A review of studies found that women who received a medicine called GnRH agonist before trying to get pregnant had more chances of getting pregnant successfully. Specifically, they had almost nine times more chances of having a baby survive and grow inside them compared to those who didn't take the medicine. However, the studies weren't perfect because some parts were hard to compare. Also, there wasn't enough information about whether the medicine might cause problems during pregnancy or after. Women with a condition called endometriosis who took this medicine for about three to six months before trying to have a baby had better chances of becoming pregnant. But we don't know yet if this medicine has any bad effects on the mother or the baby.

output: This review looked at 46 studies about different types of fainting spells. It found that some medicines like beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and anticholinergics might help prevent fainting during a special test called head-up tilt. But for another type of fainting caused by pressing on a neck area, a medicine called midodrine seemed to work better than a sugar pill in one study. The review couldn't find enough strong proof to recommend any medicines or devices for preventing these fainting spells. More studies are needed that focus on how well these treatments actually help people feel better.

output: A study looked at a vaccine for herpes zoster, which is a painful rash that can happen after chicken pox. It involved 38,546 people, mostly older adults and mostly white people. The vaccine worked well in preventing herpes zoster, which is good. But it didn't seem to help prevent a condition called postherpetic neuralgia, which causes pain after the rash goes away. The vaccine did cause some side effects at the injection site, like soreness, but these went away quickly. Serious side effects were very rare. While we don't have strong proof that the vaccine stops postherpetic neuralgia, it seems safe and helpful in preventing herpes zoster, especially in older adults.

This review looked at some studies about different ways to keep embryos safe before they're used for pregnancy. No new studies were found, so we're using the information from a previous review done in 2002. That review found two studies that looked at different methods:

- One study compared keeping embryos frozen (cryopreservation) with giving women a special liquid called human albumin through their veins. The results showed no difference between these two methods for helping women get pregnant.

- Another study compared keeping all embryos frozen and then transferring them later to the uterus (elective cryopreservation) with transferring fresh embryos right away. Again, there was no difference in how well this helped women get pregnant.

The review team concluded that there isn't enough good information to decide whether it's better to freeze embryos or give women albumin. So, they think we don't have strong proof to suggest one method is clearly better than the other.

output: A review looked at two small studies that tested Gingko biloba extract on people with AMD, which is a condition that can make it hard to see clearly. In one study, 20 people took Gingko biloba twice a day for six months, while another group took a sugar pill. In the other study, 99 people took different amounts of Gingko biloba for six months. Both studies found that Gingko biloba might help with vision problems, but the results couldn't be combined because the studies were too small. The studies didn't look at how Gingko biloba affects other parts of people's lives or if it helps stop the disease from getting worse. Some people use Gingko biloba in China, Germany, and France. More research is needed with bigger groups of people over a longer time to know if Gingko biloba really helps with AMD.

output: This review looked at 14 studies involving 1071 babies. Most of the studies were small and had some problems. When breast milk was given extra nutrients, babies grew faster in the hospital. They also got bigger in their legs and heads. But we don't know if this helps babies grow better after they leave the hospital. There's not much information about how well these babies do as they get older. The studies didn't find that giving extra nutrients made babies sicker. Also, there wasn't enough information to say if this helped or hurt babies' chances of getting a serious stomach problem called necrotizing enterocolitis. Overall, the evidence isn't very strong, but giving extra nutrients to breast milk might help babies grow a little bit faster while they're in the hospital.

This review looked at 12 studies to see if family-based programs help reduce drinking problems. But the studies weren't very good, so it's hard to know for sure. Only 20% of the studies did a good job of making sure people got the right treatment. About half of the studies had enough information to show if the programs worked, but some didn't have clear details.

Nine out of twelve studies showed that these family programs helped a little bit, and the benefits stayed for a while after the program ended. But four of those studies focused just on girls, and they seemed to work well. One study that had fewer people in it said the programs helped, but the results weren't strong enough to be certain. Two bigger studies didn't find much difference from regular care.

Overall, the review suggests that family-based programs can help a little with drinking problems, and the benefits seem to last. But more research is needed to be really sure.

output: This review looked at three studies to see if a type of medicine called TCHP helps people with chest pain called angina. The studies had different ways of doing things, and some weren't as strong as others. One study found that TCHP might help more than another medicine called nitrates, but it only had a few people in it. Two other studies said that both medicines caused some side effects, but they didn't give details. Because there aren't many studies and the ones that do exist have small groups of people, we don't know if TCHP really works well for angina. We also don't know if it's safe. More high-quality studies are needed to learn more about how effective and safe TCHP is for treating angina. So, doctors should use it carefully until we have better proof.

output: A study looked at when to do surgery after a serious brain injury called an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. The study found that people who had surgery soon after their bleeding started did much better three months later compared to those who waited longer. But it's not clear if people who had surgery between these two times also did better. The study is based on just one big experiment done a long time ago, so we can't be totally sure about the results today. Today, doctors usually try to operate on these patients within 3 to 4 days after the bleeding starts, especially if the patient isn't too sick. But more research is needed to know the best time to operate for patients who are sicker.

output: A study looked at whether a hepatitis B vaccine works well for people living with HIV who take medicine to treat their HIV. The study had 26 people who were taking medicine for HIV and had hepatitis B. They gave some people the vaccine and others a sugar pill to compare. After 12 months, everyone got good responses to the vaccine, and there were no bad side effects. But after stopping the HIV medicine, the body didn't remember the vaccine anymore. The study was small and only done in places where lots of money is available. Because of this, we don't have enough information to say if the vaccine works well for everyone with HIV. We also can't say it's dangerous. More studies need to be done in places where many people have both HIV and hepatitis B, using different ways to give the vaccine.

These studies compared a medicine called metoclopramide to nothing or to another medicine to help put a feeding tube through the nose into the stomach. The studies gave metoclopramide at different doses—either 10 milligrams or 20 milligrams. None of the studies found that metoclopramide helped more than the other medicine or nothing in helping to put the tube in the right place. Because of this, the researchers think there might not be much point in doing bigger studies to see if metoclopramide helps. They suggest that future studies need to have many more people to get clearer answers.

output:
This review looked at 32 studies involving 3,560 people to see how well catheter ablation (CA) works compared to other treatments for a condition called atrial fibrillation (AF). The studies were small and not very good, so we can't be sure about the results. 

CA seemed to help stop AF from coming back more often than other treatments did. But it's hard to know if this is true because the studies didn't agree on everything. CA also helped get the heart back into a normal rhythm in some cases, but again, the studies weren't all the same.

CA didn't seem to make people live longer or have fewer dangerous blood clots. It also didn't seem to cause more deaths from blood clots. Different types of CA didn't show one way was clearly better than the others.

Overall, CA might be a good choice for treating AF, especially when it keeps coming back. But we don't know which type of CA is best. More research is needed to figure that out.

Also, some of the studies didn't follow proper methods, like not giving people a break before starting the new treatment. Only one study had enough people to be sure about its results. This single study showed that some people taking amantadine had side effects like feeling confused or having swelling in their feet. Because of these problems, we don't know if amantadine is a good treatment for the shaking movements caused by levodopa. More research is needed to find out.

output: This review looked at studies about using adrenaline to treat anaphylaxis, but couldn't find any that met the criteria. Because of this, the review couldn't make new suggestions about when to use adrenaline. There's a need for more studies, but it's hard to do them safely. These studies would have to give people adrenaline and compare it to a fake treatment, which might not be ethical since adrenaline can save lives quickly. It's also tricky to measure how well it works because anaphylaxis happens suddenly and varies in strength. So, while the review doesn't have strong proof, it still suggests that adrenaline should be used right away for treating anaphylaxis.

output: This review looked at nine studies involving 3519 patients to see which treatment—open heart surgery called CABG or putting stents in arteries—was better. The studies compared how well these treatments worked after one year and three years. They found that CABG (open heart surgery) seemed to work better overall, especially in reducing the need for more surgeries. CABG helped reduce the chances of having another heart attack or needing another operation. But the studies weren't perfect because they didn't follow people long enough, and some of the patients might not have been typical. More research is needed to find out who might benefit more from each treatment.

output: This review looked at 23 studies with 1075 people who took omega-3 fatty acids. They found that people taking omega-3s had lower triglycerides and VLDL cholesterol compared to before. Triglycerides went down by about 0.58 mmol/L, which is a lot. VLDL cholesterol went down by about 0.07 mmol/L, though this wasn't always seen. LDL cholesterol, which can be bad for your heart, went up by about 0.11 mmol/L. There was no clear change in other things like total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, blood sugar, or how much you weigh. The study didn't find any side effects from taking omega-3s. While omega-3s helped with some fats in the blood, it didn't seem to help with blood sugar control. More studies are needed to see if omega-3s affect heart problems or death.

output: This review looked at how two medicines, chlorpromazine and penfluridol, affect people who have certain health problems. It included three studies with 130 people in total. The studies didn't show that one medicine was better than the other for keeping people out of the hospital. They also didn't find a clear difference in how often people got a feeling called akathisia. Many people left the studies early because of side effects. But people taking chlorpromazine needed fewer extra medicines to help with shaking hands and feet. The studies weren't very strong, so we can't be sure which medicine works better. More studies would help us know more clearly. If doctors use these medicines, they should do good studies to learn more.

output: A review looked at how well community mental health teams (CMHTs) help people who need mental health support. They didn't find strong proof that CMHTs make people less likely to die by suicide or in suspicious ways. But they did see that fewer people left the study early when using CMHTs. More people in the CMHT group said they were happy with their services compared to those getting regular care. There were also fewer hospital stays for people in the CMHT group. However, the review says there isn't enough strong evidence to know if CMHTs really work better than usual care. Still, it seems like CMHTs might help more people feel better about their treatment and stay out of hospitals. But the review notes that while this is good news, we still need more research to be sure.

output: This review looked at nine studies with 7960 women to see if certain ways of helping people choose a birth control method called an IUD worked. The studies found that when community helpers talked about the IUD more, more women chose it. Also, when doctors talked to women during their first visit after giving birth, more women chose the IUD. However, other ways of talking to women didn't seem to work better than usual care. The IUD is a very good way to prevent pregnancy, so healthcare providers might want to try these new ways of talking to help more women use it. But we need to look at how much it costs too, because sometimes it might not be worth it.

output: A review looked at how well people with a breathing problem called COPD do when they get treatment at home instead of in a hospital. They studied eight groups of people who had this problem and found that those who got treatment at home had fewer times when they had to go back to the hospital. This was a small but important difference, like getting a gold star on your homework instead of just a checkmark. The review also saw that people who stayed at home might live a little longer, but it wasn't clear if this was really true or just a bit of luck. There wasn't enough good information to know if staying at home helped more with things like feeling better or how strong their lungs are. So, doctors think it might be safe to treat some people at home if they have trouble breathing suddenly, especially if they have help from nurses.

Five other studies compared IPC with regular bandages that put pressure on the area. Two of these found that IPC worked better than just using bandages. But the other three didn't find a clear difference. Two studies found that IPC didn't work better than regular bandages alone.

This review looked at how street lights affect car accidents. It found 17 studies that looked at crash numbers before and after adding street lights. Most of these studies weren't very good. 

The studies showed that street lights might help reduce crashes overall. When comparing street lights to areas without lights, there were fewer crashes overall. But it's not clear if street lights make a big difference because some studies didn't find a clear effect.

Street lights also seemed to lower the number of serious crashes and deaths. When comparing street lights to daytime conditions, there were fewer crashes and deaths. But again, more studies are needed to be sure about this.

Overall, the review suggests that street lights might help keep people safer on the roads, but we need better studies to know for sure, especially in places where money isn't as available.

output: A review looked at four studies comparing a type of medicine called beta-blockers with a placebo in people with a condition called idiopathic Parkinson's disease. These studies were done in a way that mixed up who got which medicine to make sure neither group knew who had what. However, three of the studies didn't show enough information to know how well the medicine worked or if it was safe. The fourth study showed that some people had their heart rate drop lower than normal when taking the medicine, and one person stopped taking it because their heart rate became very slow. Because there wasn't enough clear information, we can't say for sure if beta-blockers help with shaking in Parkinson's disease or if they're safe. The study also found that some people's hearts beat very slowly, which might be a concern for older adults who don't usually have slow hearts. But since the study was small, we can't know for certain how big this problem might be.

A study looked at whether giving two vaccines—23-valent pneumococcal (PV) and influenza vaccines—to people with lung problems called bronchiectasis helps them feel better. They gave the PV vaccine to 167 adults with these lung issues and compared it to just the influenza vaccine. The PV vaccine seemed to help reduce times when their breathing got worse from infections. However, it didn't seem to stop them from getting pneumonia more often. Also, there wasn’t enough information about how well the vaccine helped their lungs over time.

Another study found that the PV vaccine might make the germs causing lung infections less common in kids' spit, but it didn’t show that the kids felt better overall.

So far, the best evidence suggests that the PV vaccine can be used as part of regular care for adults with bronchiectasis. For kids, there’s some support too, but more studies are needed to know for sure. We don’t have clear answers yet about how often the vaccine should be given, so doctors follow the advice from their country's healthcare guidelines.

This review looked at how well different types of ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) work to lower blood pressure. It studied 46 studies with 13,451 people who had high blood pressure. The studies showed that none of the ARBs were much better or worse at lowering blood pressure than others. 

The most effective doses were half or a quarter of the highest dose doctors usually recommend. These doses lowered blood pressure about 60 to 70% as much as the highest dose. Taking even more than the highest dose didn’t make a big difference.

The review found that all ARBs worked similarly to reduce blood pressure. They lowered it by about 8 mm Hg for systolic blood pressure (the top number) and 5 mm Hg for diastolic blood pressure (the bottom number). This happens within 1 to 12 hours after taking the medicine.

However, the review couldn't tell us much about any bad side effects because the studies weren't long enough or detailed enough about what happened to the people taking the medicines. So we know the ARBs help lower blood pressure, but we don't have a clear picture of how often they cause problems.

The review found that all ARBs worked similarly to reduce blood pressure. They lowered it by about 8 mm Hg for systolic blood pressure (the top number) and 5 mm Hg for diastolic blood pressure (the bottom number). This happens within 1 to 12 hours after taking the medicine.

However, the review couldn't tell us much about any bad side effects because the studies weren't long enough or detailed enough about what happened to the people taking the medicines. So we know the ARBs help lower blood pressure, but we don't have a clear picture of how often they cause problems.

This review looked at three studies involving 184 people who had their shoulders fixed after getting hurt. These people had a type of shoulder problem called unidirectional anterior shoulder instability. The studies compared two types of surgery: arthroscopic surgery and open surgery. Both surgeries aim to fix something called Bankart lesions, which can cause shoulder problems.

The studies didn't have enough details to be sure about their results, so it's hard to know if one type of surgery is better than the other. They found that both types of surgery worked equally well in preventing the shoulder from coming loose again or needing more surgery. However, the studies weren't very clear, so we can't be certain about these results.

For other things like how well the shoulder works, the studies didn't find big differences between the two types of surgery. More research is needed to compare these surgeries and to look at longer-term results. Researchers need to do better studies with more people and use tools to measure how well the shoulder works over time.

output: This review looked at three small studies involving 170 people to see if certain Chinese herbal medicines helped lower a type of fat in the blood called triglycerides. These studies used different herbs like Zhusuan Huoxue, Huoxue Huayu Tongluo, and Chushi Huayu. All three studies found that taking these herbs lowered triglycerides more than usual care. But the studies weren't perfect, so we can't be totally sure how well the herbs work. They didn't find any serious side effects from taking the herbs. While the herbs seem to help with triglycerides, we don't know for sure because the studies weren't very good and didn't look at long-term effects. So, while it looks promising, we need more research to be confident about the benefits.

output: This review looked at 23 studies about training for motorcycle riders. Some studies said mandatory training before getting a license might make it harder to get a license, but it didn't show if this training actually helps prevent crashes, injuries, or breaking traffic laws. Other studies looked at different kinds of training, but most had problems like not being fair in how they compared groups, not using good ways to measure if riders got better, and having too few people in the studies. Because the studies weren't very good, we can't say if training helps or hurts. We know some kind of training is probably needed, but more careful research is needed to figure out which type works best.

output: This review looked at different ways to remove a woman's uterus, called a hysterectomy. It found that after two years, women who had a subtotal hysterectomy didn't have better or worse urinary, bowel, or sexual problems compared to those who had a total hysterectomy. The surgery took about 11 minutes less and caused less bleeding. Women who had the subtotal hysterectomy were less likely to get a fever or have trouble peeing right after surgery. However, they were more likely to bleed again after their period for up to a year. The review also found that both types of surgery—done through the belly or a small cut in the belly—were similar in how well they worked overall. But the studies looking at the small cut method weren't strong enough to show all the differences clearly. Overall, this review suggests that subtotal hysterectomy doesn't offer better results for urinary, bowel, or sexual health than total hysterectomy.

output:
This review looked at ten studies with 544 people who had sudden asthma attacks. Seven studies were about adults and three were just for kids. Three studies were considered very good. They tested how well breathing air mixed with helium and oxygen helped people breathe better.

When they put all the studies together, they didn't find strong proof that it helped overall. But they did see that it might help people who already had really hard time breathing. This is based on a few studies though, so we can't be totally sure.

The studies also didn't show that using heliox made people less likely to need to go to the hospital. When they compared different doses or types of people, there wasn't much difference either.

Overall, the review says that right now, heliox isn't helpful for treating all people with sudden asthma. But it might help some people who are really sick. More research is needed to know for sure. So doctors don't usually use heliox to treat asthma attacks yet.

output: A review looked at seven studies involving 1919 people who do sports regularly. Most of the studies had some problems, like not being very clear about how they were done. Four studies focused on ways to stop hamstring injuries, which are common in sports. Two of these studies found that special exercises to strengthen the hamstrings didn't help prevent injuries. Another study suggested that getting hands-on treatment from a therapist might help, but the results weren't strong enough to be sure. Other studies tried different methods like warming up and cooling down, but none showed that these helped prevent hamstring injuries. Overall, there isn't enough good evidence to know if any specific methods work best to stop hamstring injuries in sports. More research is needed to confirm whether getting hands-on treatment can help.

output: This review looked at how well dental restorations last when using different methods to keep things dry during the procedure. Four studies with 1270 people were studied, but some of the information wasn't clear. The studies found that when dentists use something called a rubber dam to keep water away from the teeth, the restorations stay in better shape longer than when they use a cotton roll. This happened especially for kids getting fillings in their back teeth. Using the rubber dam also seemed to make the filling process faster. But the studies weren't perfect, so we can't be totally sure about these findings. More research is needed to see if this works for all types of fillings and if it's worth the extra cost.

output: This review looked at six studies with almost 450 patients to see which treatment worked better for people with a certain kind of leg problem. Most of the studies were done well. After a year, more people had their legs saved when they got special electrical devices (SCS) compared to just resting their legs. The SCS also helped people feel less pain and made them heal faster. However, using the SCS can cause some small problems like the device not working right or getting infected. These problems happened in about 15% of people who got the SCS. The SCS cost more money, around €36,500 over two years, while just resting the leg cost about €28,600. So, the SCS might help save more legs and make people feel better, but it's a bit more expensive and can have some small risks.

output:
This review looked at how well different types of antibiotics work for treating lung problems. It included 40 studies with 1717 people. Most of the studies weren't very good, so we can't be sure about their results. Overall, people who got a mix of antibiotics seemed to get better faster than those who just got one kind, but this isn't clear because the studies weren't strong. When only looking at four studies where people didn't get a fake medicine, there wasn't much difference. 

The studies didn't find that any type of antibiotic worked better than others. They also didn't look at how well people felt or how much they weighed. Some studies showed that people didn't have more bad side effects from the antibiotics. 

The review couldn't tell us which way of giving the antibiotics (like through a vein or by breathing it in) was best. We still don't know why some people don't get better even when taking antibiotics. More research is needed to understand this better.

output: This review looked at 16 studies involving 1,116 children to see if shorter or longer courses of antibiotics work better for treating urinary tract infections (UTIs) in kids. The studies found that giving kids antibiotics for 10 days instead of just one dose helps keep their pee clear of bacteria longer. About 24% of kids who got just one dose of antibiotics still had bacteria in their pee after treatment, but only 10% of those who got 10 days of antibiotics did. There wasn't much difference between the two groups when it came to other things like whether the infection came back or if the kids felt better. The review couldn't find enough information to know which antibiotic works best or if longer treatment is really better. So while 10 days of antibiotics seems to be better at getting rid of bacteria, we don't have enough strong evidence to say which antibiotic or how long to take it is best for treating UTIs in kids.

output: This review looked at two studies that compared a treatment called in vitro maturation (IVM) with another called in vitro fertilization (IVF) for women who have a condition called polycystic ovarian syndrome. Both studies had some problems following their plans, so we can't be sure how well they worked. The studies didn't find clear evidence about whether IVM helps more than IVF in terms of having a baby. However, they did find that fewer women got a problem called ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with IVM compared to IVF. More studies are needed to know if IVM is better or if it works as well as IVF. Until then, doctors don't have enough strong proof to recommend IVM over IVF for these women.

output: A review of studies found that iron does not seem to cause more cases of malaria overall. However, it's not clear if iron causes more or less malaria in places where people often have low iron levels compared to places where they don't. In areas where there are ways to prevent and treat malaria, taking iron pills doesn't seem to make malaria more common. But in places where these services aren't available, iron might make malaria slightly more common. Taking iron doesn't seem to cause more severe malaria. There were no extra deaths reported in the studies. Iron helps keep more children from having low iron levels, and their blood gets healthier after taking iron. When there are good ways to stop malaria, giving iron doesn't seem to cause more malaria. So, in places where malaria is hard to control, you can give iron to children without checking if they need it first.

This review looked at different medicines used to treat a skin condition called erythema nodosum-like lesions (ENL). It included 13 studies with 445 people. The studies weren't very good, so we couldn't combine their results easily. 

Thalidomide seemed to help more than aspirin by making the skin better. Clofazimine worked better than prednisolone at stopping the skin problems from getting worse. But thalidomide helped less when it came to the skin problems coming back. Betamethasone didn't seem to help as much as dextrose. Pentoxifylline didn't help as much as thalidomide, and indomethacin didn't help as much as prednisolone, aspirin, or chloroquine. Levamisole didn't help as much as a placebo.

Taking 100 mg of thalidomide each day had fewer side effects than taking 300 mg. More people had side effects from taking clofazimine than from taking prednisolone.

The studies didn't look at how well people felt or how much it cost to treat the condition. We need bigger and better studies to know if these medicines really work.

This review looked at 14 studies involving 2782 patients with febrile neutropenia, which is when people with weakened immune systems get a fever. The studies tested whether adding certain antibiotics called glycopeptides could help. These antibiotics are used to fight bacteria. 

In most cases, the studies didn't find that adding these antibiotics helped reduce deaths or made it less likely that the illness would come back. However, they did find that these antibiotics might make it less likely that the infection would keep going, especially when doctors changed treatments based on how the patient was doing.

The studies also showed that these antibiotics didn't cause more fungus infections. They did seem to help stop some types of bacteria from growing too much in the body. But the studies weren't perfect, so we can't be sure about all the details. Overall, the evidence suggests that adding these antibiotics doesn't seem to help save lives or prevent infections in people with cancer who have this condition.

Overall, mirtazapine seems to work well for depression, but it has different side effects compared to other medicines.

output: This review looked at 98 studies about a quick test called RADT to check for a type of bacteria called GAS in children. Most of the studies weren't very good at showing how well the test works. When all the studies were put together, the RADT test was pretty good at finding GAS, but it wasn't perfect. It correctly identified GAS in about 85 out of every 100 cases, and it correctly said there was no GAS in about 95 out of every 100 cases where there really wasn't any. This means the test isn't always right, but it's usually close. The other two tests, EIA and OIA, work about the same way. The RADT test is very good at making sure there really isn't GAS, so doctors don't give kids extra medicine they don't need. If 100 children have GAS, the test might miss 43 of them, but that's still better than just guessing. So, the RADT test can help doctors decide if a child needs medicine for GAS or not.

This review looked at 16 studies involving 72,368 people who had nodules in their thyroid glands. These studies tested a hormone called calcitonin to see if it could help find a rare type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid cancer (MTC). The tests were mostly done to decide if someone might have MTC. 

The studies found that calcitonin tests are very good at ruling out MTC, meaning they correctly say most people don't have it. But when they do find something, it's usually MTC. The problem is that many of the studies didn't have enough information to know how well the tests work, so we can't be sure about everything they found.

For the test that looks at calcitonin levels once, it's really good at catching MTC, but it also misses some cases. If the test shows a certain level of calcitonin, it means there's a 7.7% chance the person has MTC, but this number could be lower. When looking at both the first test and another test, the chances of finding MTC are even higher.

While these tests are very good at finding MTC, they're not very good at telling us if the test will help someone with thyroid nodules. Because MTC is rare, the test often finds it in people who don't need treatment right away. Also, we don't know if doing these tests helps people with MTC live longer. So, whether these tests should be used regularly for people with thyroid nodules is still uncertain.

output: This review looked at four studies about massage therapy for people living with HIV/AIDS. These studies were mixed, looking at different ages and in different types of care settings. They measured how well people felt and their immune system health. The studies showed that when massage therapy was used along with other ways to manage stress, like meditation, it helped people feel better overall. People also seemed to use less healthcare and feel more spiritually connected. Some studies found that massage therapy might help boost certain parts of the immune system. However, the studies weren't perfect and didn't always report all the side effects. While there's some good news, the evidence isn't strong enough yet to recommend massage therapy widely. More research with bigger groups of people would be helpful to know if massage really helps.

This review looked at four studies from different places like Denmark, France, Hong Kong, and the UK. These studies tested a treatment called ILM peeling, which is done during eye surgeries. The studies followed about 200 people who got this treatment and another group that didn't get it. 

The main finding was that after three months, people who got the ILM peeling did better seeing things far away. But after six months, there wasn't much difference in how well people could see. Also, fewer people who got the treatment needed more surgeries later.

The treatment seemed to help close a small hole in the back part of the eye, especially in the early stages. It also helped prevent needing more surgeries. The treatment didn't cause more problems during or after the operation.

While the treatment didn't seem to make people see better right away, it was very good at keeping the eye healthy and preventing more surgeries. One study showed that this treatment might save money in the long run because it helps keep eyes healthier.

So, even though it didn't improve how well people could see right away, the treatment seems to be a good choice because it can help keep eyes healthy and avoid more surgeries.

output: This review looked at three small studies comparing older red blood cells, which were stored for more than 21 days, with newer ones that were stored for less than 21 days. The studies had some problems, so it's hard to know if older red blood cells make people sicker. In the studies, 11.11% of people who got the older cells died, compared to 4.34% of those who got the newer cells. This difference isn't very clear because the studies weren't very big. It's also not known if older red blood cells might cause other health problems. Because of these issues, there's not enough good evidence to say whether older or newer red blood cells are better for giving to sick people. More studies are needed to find out. So far, doctors can't decide if older red blood cells should be used instead of newer ones.

The studies reviewed mostly came from low-income countries and were small and had some problems in how they were done. They looked at different types of iron medicines, how much to take, and how to give them. Some showed that taking iron pills during pregnancy can help prevent a condition called anaemia, which makes people feel tired. The pills seem to make blood cells work better than when nothing is given. But the studies didn't look at how well the medicine worked for different levels of anaemia. 

There were also studies that gave iron shots into the muscle or through a vein. These seemed to make blood cells work even better than the pills. However, there were worries about some bad side effects from the shots, like getting blood clots or having allergic reactions. The studies didn't find out if these side effects happened often enough to be a problem.

Overall, while taking iron pills seems to help with anaemia, it can cause stomach upset. Iron shots might work better, but doctors aren't sure if the benefits outweigh the risks. More studies are needed to know more about how well these treatments work and if they have serious side effects.

output: This review looked at six studies to see if giving a substance called lactoferrin to babies through their food helps prevent certain sicknesses. The studies showed that giving lactoferrin might help reduce a type of sickness called late-onset sepsis and another condition called NEC, especially in very small babies. However, it didn't seem to affect how many babies died overall. When lactoferrin was given along with something called probiotics, which are good bacteria, it seemed to work even better at preventing these sicknesses. But again, it didn't change how many babies died. Giving lactoferrin with probiotics also helped prevent some other types of sickness caused by germs. No serious side effects were seen, but we don't know about long-term health effects like brain development. More studies are needed to learn more about the best way to use lactoferrin and how it affects babies over time.

output: This review looked at 63 studies involving 9168 people who had strokes. Most of the studies didn't follow people after the treatment ended. About half of the studies said people with depression could take certain medicines called SSRIs. But the studies had different lengths, types of medicine, and doses. Only three studies were done well enough to trust their results. These three studies found that SSRIs didn't help people recover better from strokes. They also didn't find that SSRIs made it harder for people to get better. However, SSRIs did make some people have more stomach problems. One big study called FOCUS showed that SSRIs might help a bit with how much trouble people have doing daily activities. But this wasn't true for helping people be independent. Many more studies are being done now, and when those finish, we'll know more about whether SSRIs help after strokes. Right now, there's not enough good evidence to say SSRIs should be used to help people recover from strokes.

output:
This review looked at five studies that tested different ways to help people with chronic pain use less prescription painkillers called opioids. The studies tried things like acupuncture, mindfulness exercises, and talking therapies. They found mixed results. Some studies showed that people who got these special treatments used less painkillers after the studies ended. But other studies didn't see much difference between those who got the special treatments and those who didn't. 

The studies had some problems, though. They weren't very big, and it's hard to know if the results mean anything because of that. Also, some studies said people might have had side effects from the treatments. 

Overall, the studies didn't find strong proof that any of these special treatments work better than just using painkillers. There aren't many studies on this topic, so we can't be sure if these treatments really help people cut back on painkillers. The results seem to show that sometimes people do use less painkillers when they try these treatments, but it's not clear if that's because of the treatments or just chance.

output: This review looked at 44 studies involving 52 different ways of giving people advice on their diet compared to not giving them any advice. The studies followed about 18,000 people for up to 24 months. They found that people who got diet advice had slightly lower levels of total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol, which are types of fats in the blood that can build up in your arteries. Their blood pressure also went down a little bit, and they took in less salt. However, the studies didn't show clear results for other things like HDL cholesterol and triglycerides. Some studies showed that people ate more fruits and vegetables and had more fiber in their diets when they got diet advice. But it's hard to know if this advice really made a big difference because some of the studies had problems with how they collected information. The studies that looked at whether diet advice helped prevent heart problems weren't very precise, but they did suggest that reducing salt might help. Overall, diet advice seems to help make people healthier in the short term, but we don't know yet if it makes a big difference over a long time.

Lithium seemed to help prevent mood swings better than the placebo, especially for people with bipolar disorder. For people with unipolar disorder, lithium also helped, but the results weren't strong enough to be certain. The studies had some differences, which might explain why the results weren't always clear. Lithium didn’t seem to cause any bad side effects. However, there wasn’t enough information to know if lithium helps prevent suicide. More studies are needed to compare lithium with other treatments and to look at how well it prevents suicide.

This review looked at three small studies with a total of 50 people who took different amounts of a substance called resveratrol. It's a type of chemical found in some plants. The studies compared taking resveratrol to not taking it at all. None of the studies lasted very long, so we can't know if resveratrol helps or hurts people over time.

The studies didn't find clear evidence that resveratrol helps lower blood sugar levels or improve how well the body uses insulin. They also didn't find any serious side effects from taking resveratrol. However, since the studies were small and short, we can't be sure about the results.

Right now, there isn't enough good research to know if resveratrol is helpful or harmful for people with type 2 diabetes. More studies are needed to find out, especially ones that last longer and look at important things like how well people feel and how their health changes over time.

This review looked at different ways to treat people who have a flare-up of their asthma. It included eight studies with a total of 1470 adults and 470 children. The studies had mixed quality, and the severity of the asthma flare-ups varied. 

For taking medicine by mouth, there wasn't much difference between a type of medicine called LTRA and regular care. However, LTRA seemed to help improve how well a person can breathe as measured by a test called FEV1 in two studies with 641 adults. But this didn't happen in studies with children. Headaches were the most common side effect, but it didn't seem to happen more often with LTRA than with regular care.

For getting medicine through a vein, there was a slight chance that fewer people had to go to the hospital when given LTRA. This happened in two studies with 772 adults and one study with 276 children. Again, there was no clear difference in how well people could breathe as measured by FEV1. 

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to recommend using LTRA by mouth for treating asthma flares. More studies are needed to see if giving LTRA through a vein helps prevent people from going to the hospital, and to find out the best way to give it. We also need more studies to learn about its safety and effectiveness, especially for children, and to look at longer-term costs.

output: This review looked at how well a test called POCS works to find injuries in the chest and abdomen. It checked 34 studies with 8635 people. The test found about 74 out of every 100 injuries (sensitivity) and correctly said there were no injuries 96 out of 100 times (specificity). But the test wasn't always right because it depended on who was being tested and where the injury was. In children, the test found about 63 out of 100 injuries but missed some. In adults, it found about 78 out of 100 injuries and missed fewer. For chest injuries, the test was very good, finding almost all of them. But for abdominal injuries, it missed some and sometimes said there were injuries when there weren’t. If you use the test on a group of 1000 people, it might miss 73 with injuries and wrongly say 29 have injuries. In children, it might miss 118 with injuries and wrongly say 62 have injuries. The test helps doctors know if someone has chest injuries, but for abdominal injuries, it can’t be trusted alone. More tests are needed to make sure the test works well for all types of injuries.

The first study found that people who got special pacing treatments exercised longer than those who didn't get the special treatment. They also had less heart blockage and their heart function improved. But the second study didn't find much difference between getting special pacing and another treatment called TASH. Both studies had some problems, so we can't be sure how well these treatments work. More studies are needed to learn more about them.

This review looked at four studies involving children under seven years old who got special medicine to prevent a type of bacteria called Staphylococcus aureus. Two of the studies had some problems doing things fairly, while the other two did better. The most recent study didn't have many of these problems, but we're not completely sure because it's hard to know how well the study worked.

The studies found that fewer kids who got the special medicine had Staphylococcus aureus in their bodies. This is good news. But the studies weren't very clear about whether this helps or hurts the kids' lungs or overall health. They also didn't find much difference in how often kids got sick or needed extra medicine.

There was a small trend showing that kids who got the special medicine might have fewer cases of another type of bacteria called Pseudomonas aeruginosa over time. However, the studies were too short to tell if this difference is important or just a coincidence.

Overall, the studies suggest that starting the special medicine early in life and continuing it until around age six can help reduce Staphylococcus aureus in kids. But we don't know yet if this has big benefits or risks. More research is needed to understand the long-term effects and which types of medicine work best.

This review looked at 25 studies involving 3096 people to see if massage helps lower back pain. Most of the studies were done by groups that don't make money from selling things. Some used machines, while others used just a massage therapist's hands. The studies had some problems keeping things fair, so we're not sure how good they are.

For people with sudden back pain, massage helped reduce pain a bit, but didn't help them move around better. But for those with longer-lasting back pain, massage helped reduce both pain and make them move around better. Massage also helped reduce pain for people who had it for a while, even when compared to other treatments. However, these benefits didn't last very long.

Massage didn't seem to cause any major problems, but there was a small chance that it might make pain worse a little bit. Overall, we think massage might help with back pain, but we're not very confident about this. It seems to work best for reducing pain right away, but doesn't seem to help much with making movements easier.

This review looked at 53 studies that examined how well researchers report their clinical trials. It found that while many studies didn't fully explain how they did their research, some things were reported better in studies published in journals that follow guidelines set by the CONSORT statement. For example, studies in journals that follow these guidelines were more likely to say how they kept participants from knowing who was getting which treatment. 

The review also found that studies in journals following the guidelines were more likely to have good reasons for doing the study and larger groups of people in their studies. They were also more likely to use fair ways to decide who got which treatment. Overall, the review suggests that having journals follow the CONSORT guidelines can help improve how clinical trial results are reported. However, the evidence isn't strong enough to say this always happens. More studies are needed to see how effective it really is.

This review looked at 32 studies with 6075 people who had small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Most of the studies came from Europe, North America, and Asia, and they lasted from 12 to 72 months. The people in the studies were mostly around 60-65 years old. Some studies looked at people with different stages of the disease, but many didn't.

The studies didn't find that one type of medicine (called platinum-based) helped people live longer or made their tumours go away better than other types of medicines. But the people who got the platinum-based medicine had fewer tumours left after treatment, which means it might work a little bit better.

The studies also showed that the people who took the platinum-based medicine had more side effects like feeling sick, having less blood cells, and feeling tired. But these side effects weren't enough to make the medicine worse than the other medicines.

The review found that there wasn't much information about how well people felt during treatment. Future studies should try to look at how people feel while taking the medicine too.

output: This review looked at different ways to check for cervical cancer. It included over 140,000 women aged 20 to 70. Most of the studies were done well. They compared two main types of tests: one called HC2 and another called conventional cytology. HC2 is better at finding early signs of cervical problems, but it also finds more false positives. This means it might tell some women they have problems when they don't. Conventional cytology is good at finding serious problems but misses some. The HC2 test works better in Europe than in other places. Both tests are pretty good at telling if a woman has a problem, but HC2 is slightly better. A negative result on the HC2 test is usually more reliable than a negative result on the cytology test because the cytology test can sometimes be wrong. More studies are needed to know how these tests affect a woman's health overall.

output: This review looked at seven studies about exercising to help people with HIV. The studies had some differences, like how much exercise, who did it, and what they measured. Overall, the studies showed that doing exercises like lifting weights or walking at least three times a week for four weeks or more can be safe. It might help people gain a little bit of weight and muscle. Exercise also seems to improve heart and lung health. It can make people stronger and feel better mentally. But the studies weren't perfect—there weren't many of them, and some people stopped exercising before the study ended. So while the results look promising, we need more research to be sure. More studies should include different types of people and follow them longer to get clearer answers.

This review looked at four studies involving 307 people over 31 to 85 years old who had periodontitis, which is a gum problem. The studies compared different ways to clean teeth after regular treatment. Two studies used special medicines put in the mouth, and one used a light treatment. Another study compared how well dentists and doctors cleaned teeth. None of the studies looked at how many teeth people lost. Instead, they checked if gums were still healthy and if pockets around teeth got bigger.

The studies didn't find any clear differences between having a dentist or doctor do the cleaning. They also didn't find that adding medicines or light treatments helped more than just cleaning. Neither did they find that cleaning at different times worked better. 

There wasn't enough good evidence to know which way of cleaning is best. Some studies showed no difference, while others found small benefits. The results might change with more studies. So we can't say for sure which method works better. More research is needed to find out.

This review looked at many studies about tests to find out if a baby might have Down's syndrome. It included 204,759 pregnancies, which is a lot! Most of the studies were done well. Researchers looked at different tests that can help tell if a baby has Down's syndrome.

They compared lots of different test combinations, like using a mother's age and two other things called PAPP-A and free beta-hCG. This combination worked really well. It could spot about 7 out of every 10 babies with Down's syndrome, but it also might show as many as 3 out of every 10 babies who don't have it. So it's pretty good at finding the ones who do.

The review also found that adding more tests didn't seem to make the test better. There just weren't enough studies to know for sure. But the tests themselves don't hurt the mom. Some tests can make the mom feel worried because they might mean the baby could have Down's, even though it might not be true. If the mom gets a 'high risk' result, she might need to have another test called amniocentesis or CVS. These tests can help find out if the baby has Down's, but there's a small chance the baby could get sick from the test.

So, the tests are helpful, but they're not perfect. Moms need to think carefully about whether to have the extra tests after getting a 'high risk' result.

output: This review looked at whether taking folic acid, a type of vitamin, helps improve thinking skills and mood in older people. Eight studies were included, but they didn't all agree on the results. For healthy older people without problems thinking, there wasn't enough good evidence to say folic acid helps. But for older people who already had some trouble thinking, one study found that taking 800 mcg of folic acid each day for three years seemed to help with their overall thinking, memory, and how fast they process information. Another study showed that people with Alzheimer's disease might do better when given folic acid along with other medicines. Folic acid also helped lower a chemical in the blood called homocysteine. Most of the studies were small, so we don't know for sure if folic acid helps everyone. More research is needed to find out if it really works.

The review looked at 20 studies involving 1403 patients to see if inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) helped prevent people from going to the hospital for asthma attacks. The studies showed that patients who used ICS were less likely to need hospital care compared to those who didn't use it. This means fewer people had to go to the hospital—about 17 out of every 100 patients using ICS, compared to about 32 out of every 100 patients who didn't use it.

When ICS was used along with other medicines called systemic corticosteroids, it seemed to help even more. But the studies weren't all consistent, so we're not sure how much better it really makes things.

Using ICS also helped people breathe better right after taking it. It made their breathing stronger by about 7% and helped them exhale more air by about 6%. But these changes weren't big enough to make a difference in how well people felt overall.

There wasn't much information about whether ICS caused any bad side effects like shaking or feeling sick to your stomach. Overall, ICS seems to help keep people out of the hospital, but we don't know if it helps them feel better or if it works as well as other medicines.

More research is needed to figure out the best way to use ICS and who might get the most benefit from it. Using the same ways to measure how well people breathe and having everyone use the same scoring system would help make future studies clearer.

This review looked at different ways to treat a condition called Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), which causes dizzy spells. The study included 745 people who had this problem. Most of the studies were done in hospitals, but some were done by doctors in their offices.

The Epley maneuver, which is like a special head movement, helped most people feel better. It worked even better than a fake maneuver or doing nothing. About half of the people who got the Epley maneuver felt much better, compared to about a quarter before.

The Epley maneuver also made it less likely that the dizziness would come back. But it didn't work as well as another maneuver called the Semont maneuver. The Brandt-Daroff exercises, which involve moving your head around, weren't as good as the Epley maneuver.

The Epley maneuver is safe, but some people might feel sick during the movements. Also, the dizziness can come back after treatment.

Overall, the Epley maneuver seems to be a good way to help with BPPV. It's not perfect though, because the dizziness often comes back.

It found that internet programs that are personalized and interactive seem to work better than regular internet programs after six months or longer. These programs helped people quit smoking more often. But it's not clear if this works for younger people. Some of the studies had problems that might have affected their results. Overall, the evidence isn't very strong, so we need more research to know if these internet programs really help everyone stop smoking.

output: This review looked at 10 studies involving 898 people who took a plant called Radix Sophorae flavescentis. Most of the studies were not done very well. They compared this plant to other medicines used for hepatitis B. The studies didn't tell us if the plant helped or hurt people's health. They also didn't tell us if the plant made people feel better or worse. The plant seemed to help reduce the amount of a certain virus in some people's blood, but we're not sure if it really helps overall. There were some problems with how the studies were done, so we can't be very confident about the results. It's important to do more studies to find out if this plant actually works and if it's safe. Until then, we shouldn't rely too much on this plant for treating hepatitis B.

output: This review looked at studies comparing acupuncture and acupressure to other treatments for menstrual pain. It included 42 research studies involving 4640 women. For acupuncture, some studies showed it might help reduce pain, but others didn't find a difference. The studies had mixed results, and the quality of the evidence wasn't strong. Acupuncture seemed to work better than a fake treatment or no treatment at all. But when comparing acupuncture to medicines like ibuprofen, the studies weren't clear about which worked better. Acupuncture also seemed to cause fewer side effects. For acupressure, there weren't enough studies to draw firm conclusions. Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure if acupuncture or acupressure helps with menstrual pain. More research is needed to know for certain.

This review looked at eight studies involving 6,615 people to see if sending text messages could help remind people to go to their doctor’s appointments. Four new studies were added to the review. The studies showed that getting text message reminders made people go to their appointments more often than when they didn’t get any reminders. It worked just as well as getting a phone call reminder. When both text messages and mail reminders were used, more people went to their appointments. Two studies showed that teaching with special simulators helped people learn better and remember what they learned. One study found that using these simulators might help save babies' lives right after birth, but it's not clear if it helps them live longer. Another study showed that teaching with simulators could also help doctors work better together during resuscitations. However, we're not sure if these extra classes really help keep babies healthy for longer. The studies mostly happened in places where it's harder to get good medical care. More research is needed to see if these teaching methods help babies stay healthier overall and if they help with brain development.

This study looked at whether a special treatment called bronchoalveolar lavage helps babies with a lung problem called cystic fibrosis. They studied 157 children who were very young and had been diagnosed early. The study compared this special treatment to the usual way doctors treat them when their lungs get sick.

The study found that the special treatment didn't seem to help the children's lungs work better or be healthier overall. It also didn't make the children eat more food. But it did make the children stay in the hospital fewer days, even though they stayed longer than usual after each treatment.

The study couldn't find enough differences to say for sure if the special treatment helped or not. There were some small problems like the children having a little bit worse cough right after the treatment, but these weren't serious.

Overall, this study suggests that the special treatment might not be helpful for young children with cystic fibrosis. More research is needed to see if it works for older children and adults.

This review looked at different medicines to help people sleep better. It found that some medicines called SSRIs might help people sleep better after six weeks, but it's not clear if this happens for everyone. Paroxetine, which is one type of SSRI, seemed to work well for sleep problems. However, another SSRI called fluoxetine didn't seem to help much.

Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), like doxepin, also seemed to help people sleep better. They made people sleep longer and wake up less often, but they didn't make people fall asleep faster. The side effects of TCAs weren't very different from those of a sugar pill.

Some other medicines called "other" antidepressants, like trazodone, also seemed to help people sleep better. They helped people feel less sleepy when they woke up in the morning and had fewer dry mouth and thirst issues. But there wasn't enough information about how safe these medicines are, especially when taken for a long time.

Overall, the results aren't very strong because there weren't many studies. Some medicines might help people sleep better, but we need more research to know for sure. More high-quality studies are needed to learn more about these medicines for sleep problems.

This review looked at eight studies comparing acupuncture to no treatment for people with chronic hepatitis B. However, the studies had some problems, so we can't be sure about what happened. Most of the studies were done in China, and they didn't tell us how much money they got. 

The studies didn't find strong proof that acupuncture helps with serious side effects or improves how well people feel. But they did find that people who got acupuncture had lower levels of something called HBV DNA, which is a marker of the virus. This is a bit confusing because other studies haven't found this same result.

Overall, we're not very confident about what acupuncture does for people with hepatitis B. More research is needed, especially studies that use real needles instead of fake ones to see if they work better. We also need more studies that look at important things like how people feel and if the treatments cause any harm.

output: This review looked at how teaching people in communities can help save babies' lives. It included 33 different studies done in many parts of the world, mostly in Asia. These studies showed that when people get taught about being a good mom and dad, it helps keep babies healthier and safer. The teaching helped reduce the number of babies who died soon after birth (early neonatal mortality) and later (late neonatal mortality). It also helped more moms start feeding their babies right away. However, the teaching didn't seem to help moms use special tools during birth or go to doctors before their baby is born. The studies found that teaching families together worked best. Some of these teaching programs cost money, but they were still very good at saving babies' lives. The review suggests that teaching families together can be a useful way to help keep babies healthy in places where there aren't many doctors.

output:
This review looked at a small study with 22 people who have sickle cell disease (SCD) to see if a medicine called pregabalin helps with nerve pain. The study gave pregabalin to half the people and a sugar pill to the other half. Both groups took the medicine for three months. 

The study found that people taking pregabalin didn't feel less pain overall, as measured by a pain test. But their quality of life seemed to improve slightly, though it's hard to be sure about this because the study wasn't very big. The medicine didn't seem to help people sleep better. Some people had more side effects from the medicine, but it wasn't clear if this made a real difference.

Overall, the study isn't strong enough to give us a clear answer about whether pregabalin works for nerve pain in people with SCD. There just aren't many studies on this topic, so we need more research to know if this medicine might help.

output: The review looked at nine studies with a total of 692 people to see how well different medicines helped reduce agitation and behavior problems in people with dementia. Some medicines called SSRIs seemed to help reduce agitation, as shown by a test called the Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory. However, the results weren't always clear because one big study had a big impact. Other medicines like citalopram and trazodone didn't seem to make much difference in reducing agitation. But all the medicines seemed to work as well as each other in terms of causing side effects. More studies are needed to know if these medicines are good choices for treating agitation and behavior problems in dementia.

output: This review looked at different treatments for people who have been very sick and need help breathing. It found that giving extra insulin (a medicine to control blood sugar) can help reduce how long someone needs to stay in the hospital and also helps them breathe better. But using more insulin can sometimes make blood sugar too low, which can be dangerous. Another treatment that might help is giving people exercises early on to move around, but the results weren't clear. Some people think that giving certain medicines called steroids might help, but the review couldn't find strong proof either way. The review also said that doctors need to use the same way to check if someone has a sickness in their lungs to get more accurate results. More big studies are needed to learn more about these treatments.

output: This review looked at how well different tests can spot a condition called glaucoma. It checked 106 studies that looked at 16,260 eyes. The tests used were GDx, HRT, and OCT. GDx had the best results, with a sensitivity of 67% and a specificity of 94%. This means it correctly identified 67% of people with glaucoma and 94% of people without it. However, when using a sensitivity of 70% and a high specificity of around 95%, the tests might miss about 60 out of 200 people with glaucoma and incorrectly refer about 50 out of 800 people without it. The accuracy varied depending on how severe the glaucoma was. Overall, the tests seem to work similarly, but more research is needed to get a clearer picture. The studies had some problems, like using people who were already being seen by doctors, which might make the results less useful. Researchers suggest doing new studies with a wider range of people and reporting specific details about the tests.

output:
This review looked at 27 studies involving 8244 people who had surgery. The studies compared different types of medicine called nitrates (like nitroglycerin and isosorbide dinitrate) with no treatment, a sugar pill, or other medicines. Most of the surgeries were considered low to moderate risk for heart problems.

The studies didn't find much difference in how long people lived after their surgery when they took nitrates compared to not taking them. They also didn't find a big difference in things like chest pain, heart attacks, or heart failure. 

However, some studies suggested that a specific nitrate called nicorandil might help prevent certain heart problems. But the evidence wasn't strong enough to be sure about this.

output: This review looked at seven studies involving 1839 people who had blood clots and were being treated at home or in hospitals. Most of the studies had some problems, like not treating everyone equally. The studies found that people treated at home with a medicine called LMWH had fewer blood clots come back compared to those treated in hospitals with another medicine called UFH. There wasn't much difference in how often people got big or small injuries from the medicines. The studies also didn't find a clear difference in how long people lived. Some people felt better when they were treated at home. But there wasn't enough strong evidence to say for sure which treatment was best. Because more people are being treated at home now, doctors are working on making rules to help with this kind of treatment.

output:
This review looked at how well three different medicines—chlorpromazine, olanzapine, risperidone, and quetiapine—work for treating certain mental health problems. The studies didn't look at how much money it costs to use these medicines.

In the short term, which means for a few weeks to months, olanzapine seemed to work better than chlorpromazine. People taking olanzapine had more good responses to their treatment. But there wasn't much difference between olanzapine and the other medicines in terms of making people feel better overall or having fewer side effects like movement problems.

Risperidone and quetiapine didn't seem to work any better than chlorpromazine in the short term. Both medicines helped people feel better, but there weren't enough differences to say which one was better. Neither medicine caused more side effects like movement problems.

People taking olanzapine said they felt better overall, while those taking risperidone also said they felt better. There were no big differences in how quickly people left the studies because of side effects.

Most of the studies used people who were in hospitals in China. So the results might not apply to everyone else. The studies mostly looked at short-term use of these medicines, so we don't know how they compare over longer periods. The medicines didn't cause many serious side effects, but some people did have more movement problems when taking chlorpromazine.

The review looked at how well different treatments work for a condition called high-grade VIN, which affects the skin around the vagina. Three studies showed that a cream called imiquimod worked better than a cream with nothing in it. Women who used the imiquimod cream had more complete and partial responses to the treatment after five to six months. This happened in 58 out of 62 women using the imiquimod cream compared to none of the 42 women using the placebo cream. At 12 months, the imiquimod cream still seemed to work better, helping 38 out of 24 women compared to none of the 23 women using the placebo. But the study that used imiquimod also found that some women had to use less of the cream because it made their skin red, sore, or itchy.

One study compared imiquimod to another medicine called cidofovir. It found that both medicines worked about the same, with 57% of women responding to the imiquimod and 62% responding to cidofovir. But more women using the imiquimod cream had side effects like redness and itching.

Another study looked at a medicine called indole-3-carbinol. It found that only one woman in the indole-3-carbinol group had a complete response, while 45% of the women in the imiquimod group did. More women in the indole-3-carbinol group had side effects, but the difference wasn't very big.

Overall, imiquimod seems to be a good treatment for high-grade VIN, but we need more long-term studies to know if it works better over time. There are also other studies looking at different treatments that might help.

output: A study looked at whether using a special tool called EAUS before repairing a tear in the area around the vagina helps prevent certain problems after giving birth. They followed 752 new mothers who had a specific type of tear. The study found that using the EAUS tool might help reduce a serious problem called severe incontinence, which means leaking stool or gas that can be embarrassing. However, it also seemed to cause more pain in the first few weeks after birth. The study showed mixed results for other issues like overall discomfort and how well the tool detects something called OASIS, which can sometimes lead to problems later. While the study suggests the tool might help, it only involved a small number of women, and more research is needed to confirm these findings. More studies are needed to see if the tool works better and if it affects how women feel about their care after birth.

output:
This review looked at different ways to treat stress urinary incontinence, which is when you leak urine when you cough, laugh, or exercise. It included 55 studies with 5417 women who had the treatments. 

The main findings were:

- Open retropubic colposuspension worked well. About 69% to 88% of women didn't leak urine after the surgery.
- Women who had open retropubic colposuspension leaked less often than those who just waited or used medicine.
- Over time, fewer women leaked urine after open retropubic colposuspension compared to other surgeries.
- Compared to traditional slings, open retropubic colposuspension didn't work better in the short term, but it might be better in the long term.
- Using needles instead of traditional slings led to fewer leaks after the first year.
- The new methods like TVT and laparoscopic colposuspension might be cheaper, but we need more information about how safe and effective they are in the long run.

Overall, open retropubic colposuspension seems to be a good option, especially for long-term relief. But it can cause more prolapse and more problems with peeing. Laparoscopic colposuspension might be quicker to recover from, but we don't know yet if it's as good in the long term.

output: This review looked at five new studies, adding to twelve total studies that included 2300 people with oral cavity cancer. Most of the studies had some problems being fair, so we can't be sure how well they worked. The studies mostly compared two types of neck surgery - one done right away and another done later. They didn't find strong evidence that one type of surgery was better than the other for overall survival or disease-free survival. Some studies found that doing the surgery right away might help keep the cancer from coming back, but this wasn't always clear. Other studies found that certain types of surgery might reduce the chance of the cancer coming back. But overall, the evidence isn't very strong, so we can't say for sure which type of surgery works best. The studies also had trouble measuring side effects and quality of life after the surgeries. So, we don't have enough good information to make a clear decision about which type of neck surgery is best.

This review looked at six studies involving 681 people with asthma flare-ups. The studies used different types of medicine called antibiotics, like macrolides and penicillins. Some studies gave people antibiotics, while others gave them a sugar pill (placebo) to compare how well the antibiotics worked. The studies lasted from one to twelve weeks.

The studies mostly showed that antibiotics might help make asthma symptoms better. For example, some studies found that people who took antibiotics had fewer days when their breathing wasn't good. But other studies didn't find this effect. Also, the studies weren't perfect, so we can't be sure how well the antibiotics really work.

There wasn't enough information to know if antibiotics made it more likely for people to get sick or have other problems. Most of the people in the studies had their asthma flare-ups in the hospital, so we're not sure if the results would apply to everyone with asthma.

Overall, the evidence isn't strong enough to say for sure if antibiotics help with asthma flare-ups. More research is needed to learn more about this.

output: This review looked at 54 studies about exercise for people with knee osteoarthritis (OA). Most studies had good methods, but some parts might not be completely fair. Exercise helped reduce pain right away, making it feel less than 44 points on a 0 to 100-point scale instead of 32 points. It also helped improve how well people could move their knees, making it better than 38 points instead of 28 points. Exercise also made people feel better overall, improving their quality of life by more than 4 points. About 14% of people stopped exercising, which wasn't different from those who didn't exercise. Some people did get a little more knee or back pain from the exercise, but nothing serious happened. After stopping the exercise, pain and movement got better for about 6 to 9 points and 3 to 5 points, respectively, for up to six months. Different types of exercise programs worked differently, with individual programs often being more effective. The benefits of exercise are moderate to small, similar to what you might get from taking certain medicines. Since many people knew they were getting exercise, it's possible they felt better because of that. Overall, exercise seems to help knee OA, but more research is needed to confirm these findings.

output: This review looked at whether waiting to give antibiotics works better than giving them right away for some common illnesses like sore throats, ear infections, and colds. It included 11 studies with a total of 3555 people. Most studies showed that waiting to give antibiotics didn't make much difference in how sick people felt or how quickly they got better. However, it did find that waiting to give antibiotics led to fewer people taking antibiotics overall. This means fewer antibiotics were used when people waited, which could help stop bacteria from becoming resistant to antibiotics. Some studies also said that people who waited were just as satisfied with their care as those who got antibiotics right away. So, for some types of illness, waiting might be a good idea instead of giving antibiotics right away, especially if you're not sure about prescribing them. This can help keep more people healthy and reduce the spread of antibiotic-resistant germs.
